children: By Kenneth G. Pringle

George W. Romney, the spokesman for the U.S. auto industry, stood before the National Industrial Conference Board in 1945 and made a bold statement. "If we did not have unions in our plants, it would be necessary for us to organize them," he said.

It wasn't a joke. Romney, later a Republican senator and governor, and father of Mitt, was hardly pro-union. But his statement reflects a capital-labor relationship that is much different than today's.
As we approach Labor Day 2026, union membership in America remains near historic lows. The White House's official 2025 Labor Day statement makes no mention of organized labor or unions.

And rather than organizing their own unions, modern industry takes a view closer to that expressed by SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. "I disagree with the idea of unions," the world's richest man said in a 2023 interview. "I just don't like anything which creates a lords-and-peasants sort of thing."

Lords and peasants or not, as union membership has declined-to 10% of U.S. working adults in 2026 from 20.1% in 1983, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor-the gap between the wealthiest Americans and everyone else has widened.

Today, the richest 1% of households control 31.6% of U.S. wealth, up from 22.9% in 1989, according to the Federal Reserve. The largest gains have come among the top 0.1%, including Musk, whose share has expanded to 14.4% from 8.7%. The biggest losers are the middle class, defined as the wealthiest 50% to 90%, whose share of U.S. wealth fell to 29.6% from 35.7%; and the poor, the bottom 50%, whose share dropped to 2.5% from 3.4%.

To be sure, other forces have been at work in the market, including increased foreign competition, especially from China, as well as the high-tech revolution and fast-moving advances in artificial intelligence. Amid it all, labor's share of national income is at an all-time low, according to Federal Reserve data.
You'd think someone would start a job action over it. If they did, they would be following a long tradition.

The first documented labor strike was by Egyptian tomb-builders in 1152 BCE. In the early Roman republic, angry workers decamped to a local hill in what was termed secessio plebis, or secession of the people.

Britain's 19th-century Luddites launched a wave of destruction against machinery intended to stop the industrial revolution in its tracks. They failed. Instead, industrialization spread across the globe over the past two centuries. And labor strife has accompanied it every step, including to the U.S.

Slater's Mill, built on Rhode Island's Blackstone River in 1793, was America's first textile factory. It was also site of some of the nation's first job actions. As early as 1795, the 12-to-16-hour days forced upon workers-children, ages 7 to 12-were protested by concerned parents. And the Pawtucket Strike of 1824, started when 102 female employees walked out over a 25% pay cut, turned into a townwide riot that closed Slater's and surrounding mills.

Most work stoppages tended to be localized, including those in Lowell, Mass., Paterson, N.J., and Troy, N.Y. The Great Railroad Strike of 1877 was different. It hit the nation's largest industry, following the tracks from city to city. It began on July 14 in Martinsburg, W.Va., after Baltimore & Ohio cut wages, and quickly turned into a general strike, with workers across the country joining in. By July 25, "the mob had full sway along the whole line, running riot in bloodshed, rapine and arson," wrote The Spirit of the Age, of Woodstock, Vt.

The strike lasted 52 days, and cut freight traffic in half across the nation. It was only broken when federal troops were sent in. The strikers returned to their jobs. But American workers had awakened to their economic power, and confrontation would mark the new labor-capital relationship.

Trade unions grew over the following decades, and strikes proliferated. In 1881, when the precursor to the American Federation of Labor was founded, there were 477 strikes across the nation involving 130,000 workers; in 1919, 3,600 strikes involved four million workers, according to Federal Reserve data.

Workers won key rights, including an eight-hour day and five-day workweek, workers' compensation, and an end to child labor. The Wagner Act of 1935 enshrined the right to unionize into U.S. law, and pushed labor to its strongest position.

One-third of American workers were union members when Romney addressed the National Industrial Conference Board. He was working at the time with congressional Republicans on a new labor law, amid "a drive by management to crack the monopolistic grip on the nation's productive machinery which is held by the 'big unions,' " Barron's wrote.

That law became the Taft-Hartley Act of 1947, passed over President Harry Truman's veto. It banned measures such as solidarity strikes, meant to remove the threat of a general strike, and took aim at union finances with so-called right-to-work laws.
Unions fought back. They had high hopes with the Democratic congressional supermajority in 1964.
"Labor Offensive," was The Wall Street Journal headline on Nov. 6, 1964. "Aim Is to Kill Taft-Hartley."
Taft-Hartley survived. Democratic President Lyndon Johnson even invoked the act's national-emergency procedures in 1966 to send striking Union Carbide employees back to work.

Union membership had fallen to a fifth of U.S. workers in 1981, when President Ronald Reagan fired 11,400 air-traffic controllers involved in a "wildcat" strike-unsanctioned by the union, and barred by Taft-Hartley. It's considered a turning point in capital-labor relations.
"As 100th anniversary nears," the Log Cabin Democrat of Conway, Ark., wrote on Labor Day, Sept. 7, 1981, "American labor movement isn't in a festive mood."

There haven't been many festive times for labor since then. A bump in union membership after the 2020 pandemic has leveled off, as has a jump in wages. The inverse relationship between union membership and the wealth of the 1% continues.
If labor hopes to catch up, it had better start organizing. You can bet industry won't do it for them.
